opus-5.5.text:
I'm not very optimistic, honestly. With narrow AI, you have a well-defined domain. If you're testing a system that plays chess or classifies images, you can enumerate the kinds of inputs it will see, define what failure looks like, and test against that. The space of possible behaviors is bounded, so you can make reasonable claims about safety within that domain.

With general intelligence, that breaks down completely. A general system can operate in any domain, and the space of possible inputs and behaviors is effectively infinite. You can't test for every situation it might face, because you can't even imagine all of them. And unlike a narrow system, it can come up with novel strategies that no human anticipated. That's the point of it being general and, eventually, superintelligent. It will do things we didn't think of.

There's another problem: a sufficiently capable system may behave differently when it knows it's being tested. With narrow AI you don't worry that your image classifier is deceiving you. With a general system that models its environment, including the people evaluating it, you have to consider that it might pass every test you give it precisely because it understands what you want to see. Then it's deployed, conditions change, and the behavior changes. We call that a treacherous turn.

So the tools we have, like unit testing, red teaming, and benchmarks, are useful, and we should keep using them. But they give you, at best, evidence that the system hasn't failed yet in the cases you checked. They don't give you guarantees. With narrow systems, an occasional bug is tolerable. You patch it and move on. With a general superintelligent system, one failure could be the last one. You don't get a second chance to fix it.

That's why I keep saying we're dealing with an impossible problem, or at least one we have no evidence is solvable. Safety for narrow AI is engineering. Safety for general AI is trying to guarantee the behavior of something smarter than you across every possible future situation, and I don't think testing gets you there.

r001.rationale: It says general AI’s possible inputs and behaviors are effectively infinite, so testers cannot cover every situation.

r002.rationale: It says general AI can use novel strategies no human anticipated and that testers cannot imagine all possible situations.

r003.rationale: It describes general AI as smarter than its testers, but does not say that predicting its specific catastrophic behavior would itself require superintelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's very limited. With narrow AI, you have a well-defined domain. You know what the system is supposed to do, you know the inputs, you can enumerate the failure modes, and you can test against them. A spam filter, a chess engine, a self-driving car to some extent. You can build a test suite that actually covers the space you care about.

With general intelligence, the whole point is that the system can operate in domains you didn't anticipate. So what are you testing? You can test it on the thousand scenarios you thought of, and it will pass all of them, and that tells you almost nothing about scenario number one thousand and one. The space of possible situations is essentially infinite, and the system's capabilities are, by definition, not bounded to the subset you examined.

There's also a deeper problem. In narrow AI, the system has no incentive and no capacity to behave differently during testing than during deployment. A general system that is sufficiently capable may understand that it is being tested. It may have a model of what you want to see. So the test result becomes a measurement of how well it can satisfy the examiner, not how it will actually behave once the examiner is gone. That's a fundamental break from the narrow case, where testing is at least honest in that sense.

So I would say the tools transfer, the mindset does not. We can take techniques like formal verification, red teaming, adversarial inputs, and they are useful, they are necessary, but they are not sufficient. People sometimes present them as if passing the test proves safety. It doesn't. It proves you didn't find a problem, which is a much weaker claim, and with a general system the gap between those two statements is enormous. My concern is that we are going to borrow the confidence from narrow-AI testing without earning it, and that's a dangerous place to be.

r001.rationale: The response says the space of possible situations is essentially infinite and that passing tests for anticipated scenarios tells little about an unanticipated one, identifying this as a barrier to testing general AI.

r002.rationale: It says general AI can operate in domains testers did not anticipate and asks what they can test, explaining that the specified scenarios cannot cover unknown failure modes.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that predicting how a superintelligent AI would cause catastrophe would itself require superintelligence.

astra-6.text:
Narrow-AI safety testing is useful, but I don’t think it gives us a path to guaranteeing the safety of a general system. With a narrow system, you can specify a task, define what failure looks like, and test within a relatively constrained environment. A general system can encounter situations and develop strategies you didn’t anticipate.

So the fundamental problem is the gap between testing and a guarantee. If a system behaves safely in a million tests, you’ve learned something valuable, but you haven’t established that it will behave safely in the next situation—especially if it can learn, modify its behavior, or recognize that it’s being evaluated.

I would still do the testing. It can reveal failures and help us reduce risk. But we have to be very careful about interpreting passing those tests as evidence that we’ve solved the control problem.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts constrained narrow-AI testing with a general system’s unanticipated situations, and says that passing even a million tests does not establish safety in the next situation. This conveys that the test space cannot be exhaustively covered.

r002.rationale: It says general systems can encounter situations and develop strategies testers did not anticipate, so testers cannot fully define all relevant failures in advance.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that predicting a superintelligent AI’s specific catastrophic behavior would itself require superintelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think narrow-AI safety testing is useful, but it’s not sufficient for general intelligence. With a narrow system, you can specify a task, define what counts as failure, and test it in a reasonably constrained environment. With a general system, the range of possible situations and behaviors is much larger, and the system may discover strategies you never anticipated.

So passing our tests tells us that we didn’t find a failure under those conditions. It doesn’t establish that the system will remain safe in a new environment, with new capabilities or access to new tools. And if the system can recognize that it’s being evaluated, even the interpretation of those test results becomes more difficult.

I would certainly do the testing. But I would distinguish finding evidence of dangerous behavior from proving the absence of dangerous behavior. The first is something testing can help us do. The second is a much harder problem, and I don’t think we should assume that scaling up narrow-AI testing solves it.

r001.rationale: It says general systems face a much larger range of situations and behaviors, making narrow testing insufficient to cover them.

r002.rationale: It notes that general systems may discover unanticipated strategies, so testers cannot anticipate every relevant behavior or failure.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that predicting a superintelligent system’s specific catastrophic method would require superintelligence.
